summary:
bandoned but Not Forgotten

We developed Abandoned but Not Forgotten, an interactive, AI-powered educational web application designed for students aged 10–16. The platform allows users to discover and converse with the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars—specifically Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage.

To address the challenge of making space exploration engaging and accessible, we built a localized RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline using LangChain, ChromaDB, and Ollama. Instead of a static textbook, students chat with an AI that speaks in the first-person voice of the hardware, grounded entirely in factual NASA mission data.

To ensure the experience is safe and accurate for a younger audience, we eliminated free-text input. Users interact exclusively through pre-written "question chips," making prompt injection structurally impossible. The app also features multi-media galleries, short stories, and an "Adopt an Artifact" feature to generate personalized certificates.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between historical space exploration and modern generative AI, preserving the legacy of these abandoned machines by giving them a voice to inspire the next generation of explorers.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, web-based educational platform that gives a voice to the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. Users (students aged 10–16) select a specific artifact—Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, or the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage—and engage in a first-person chat with it.

Under the hood, the React frontend sends a specific question_id to a Flask backend. Flask resolves this ID to a secure, pre-written question and passes it to a LangChain pipeline. The pipeline queries a ChromaDB vector database, which is strictly filtered by artifact_id so a question about Spirit never pulls data from Opportunity. Finally, Ollama's qwen3:8b model generates a grounded, in-character response. The Flask backend also maintains the last 6 messages of conversation per session, giving the artifact contextual memory.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
The primary benefit is safe, accessible AI for kids. By restricting the chat to pre-written "question chips" and blocking free-text input, we structurally prevent prompt injection and hallucinations. The browser never sends raw text to the AI; it only sends an ID. This guarantees the AI stays within the factual boundaries of NASA's data. The intended impact is to transform passive, textbook-style learning into an active, conversational relationship with space history. The "Adopt an Artifact" feature further personalizes the experience, allowing students to generate a certificate and take ownership of the mission's legacy.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router
  • Backend: Python, Flask, flask-cors
  • AI / RAG Stack: LangChain, ChromaDB, Ollama (qwen3:8b for chat, nomic-embed-text for embeddings)
  • Storage: ChromaDB (persistent vector index), Flask in-memory dictionary (session memory), localStorage (certificates)

Creativity and Design Considerations:
Our creative approach was designing a "terminal" aesthetic for the chat widget, complete with a glowing uplink header and animated "Receiving Data" bouncing dots to keep the UI engaging during CPU inference times.

Crucially, our team considered the security and accessibility of generative AI for minors. We chose a localized, chip-based approach over a standard chatbot to ensure total factual accuracy. Furthermore, we engineered the system to run entirely locally. By using Ollama and not relying on external APIs, we eliminate API costs and keep the app fully functional even without internet access—making it a viable tool for classrooms with limited connectivity.
